query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: For HEA nanoparticles crystallized as a single‐phase solid solution, the maintenance of structural and chemical stability over the broad temperature range relevant to catalytic and thermoelectric applications is governed by the balance between thermodynamic driving forces (such as negative mixing enthalpy and strain due to atomic size mismatch) and kinetic barriers (notably, the activation energy for surface and bulk diffusion). When kinetic constraints are strong enough to retard elemental segregation despite increased atomic mobility at elevated temperatures, the solid solution is retained. Conversely, if the diffusion kinetics overcome these barriers, phase separation or ordering will occur.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in near‐equiatomic proportions forming a single-phase solid solution.
generation.intervention: Exposure of the HEA nanoparticles to catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions with temperature ramps and dwell times spanning 473–1923 K under controlled atmospheres.
generation.conditions: Experiments performed under inert or reaction-specific atmospheres (avoiding strong oxidizers) with well-controlled heating rates and dwell periods to simulate operating conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Interplay of mixing enthalpy, strain energy stemming from atomic size mismatch, and kinetic hindrance to atomic diffusion (surface and bulk) acts as the mediator between the retained solid solution and the onset of segregation or ordering.
generation.mechanism: At moderate operating temperatures, high configurational entropy stabilizes a homogeneous phase. However, as temperature increases, enhanced atomic mobility may trigger elemental diffusion. If the energy barriers (due to strain and local bonding effects) are sufficiently high, diffusion remains slow and the original structure persists. If these barriers are low (or if there exists an excessively negative mixing enthalpy), rapid diffusion facilitates phase separation or chemical ordering, compromising stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with an optimal balance—moderate negative mixing enthalpy and controlled atomic size mismatch—will maintain their single-phase, chemically homogeneous state across the entire temperature range. In contrast, nanoparticles with excessive size mismatch or strongly negative mixing enthalpy will exhibit observable segregation and formation of secondary phases upon exposure to high temperatures.
generation.baseline: The initial state is a well-characterized, homogeneous solid solution as confirmed by X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy before thermal treatment.
generation.boundary: This prediction holds under conditions where external factors such as reactive atmospheres or catalytic adsorbates do not independently alter diffusion kinetics. Deviations may occur in oxidative conditions or in the presence of reactive gases that modify surface energies.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative thresholds for the required kinetic barriers and the exact limits of mixing enthalpy and size mismatch that determine stability are not yet precisely defined and require systematic experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of equimolar HEA nanoparticles with systematically varied constituent elements (to adjust atomic size mismatch and mixing enthalpy). Subject each set to a controlled temperature ramp from 473 K up to 1923 K under inert atmospheres while continuously monitoring phase composition and chemical homogeneity using in situ X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy.
measurements: In situ X-ray diffraction (to detect phase transitions and peak splitting indicative of segregation)
High-resolution TEM (to visualize nanoscale phase boundaries or ordering)
EDS mapping (to monitor elemental distributions before and after thermal exposure)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles designed with moderate atomic size mismatch and mixing enthalpy unexpectedly exhibit phase segregation or chemical ordering under the prescribed thermal conditions, or if all nanoparticles (including those predicted to be stable) show no instability despite conditions theoretically favorable for overcoming kinetic barriers, then the hypothesis that kinetic barriers govern the retention of a single-phase solid solution would be falsified.

A map of single-phase high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys have exhibited unusual materials properties. The stability of equimolar single-phase solid solution of five or more elements is supposedly rare and identifying the existence of such alloys has been challenging because of the vast chemical space of possible combinations. Herein, based on high-throughput density-functional theory calculations, we construct a chemical map of single-phase equimolar high-entropy alloys by investigating over 658,000 equimolar quinary alloys through a binary regular solid-solution model. We identify 30,201 potential single-phase equimolar alloys (5% of the possible combinations) forming mainly in body-centered cubic structures. We unveil the chemistries that are likely to form high-entropy alloys, and identify the complex interplay among mixing enthalpy, intermetallics formation, and melting point that drives the formation of these solid solutions. Sub-nanometric High-Entropy Alloy Cluster: Hydrogen Spillover Driven Synthesis on CeO2 and Structural Reversibility

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles (NPs) have attracted significant attention as promising catalysts owing to the various unique synergistic effects originating from the nanometer-scale, near-equimolar mixing of five or more components to produce single-phase solid solutions. However, the study of sub-nanometer HEA clusters having sizes of less than 1 nm remains incomplete despite the possibility of novel functions related to borderline molecular states with discrete quantum energy levels. The present work demonstrates the synthesis of CeO2 nanorods (CeO2-NRs) on which sub-nanometer CoNiCuZnPd HEA clusters were formed with the aid of a pronounced hydrogen spillover effect on readily reducible CeO2 (110) facets. The CoNiCuZnPd HEA sub-nanoclusters exhibited higher activity during the reduction of NO by H2 even at low temperatures compared with the corresponding monometallic catalysts. Stability of high-entropy alloys under electrocatalytic conditions

Abstract: SummaryHigh-entropy alloys are claimed to possess superior stability due to thermodynamic contributions. However, this statement mostly lies on a hypothetical basis. In this study, we use on-line inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometer to investigate the dissolution of five representative electrocatalysts in acidic and alkaline media and a wide potential window targeting the most important applications. To address both model and applied systems, we synthesized thin films and carbon-supported nanoparticles ranging from an elemental (Pt) sample to binary (PtRu), ternary (PtRuIr), quaternary (PtRuIrRh), and quinary (PtRuIrRhPd) alloy samples. For certain metals in the high-entropy alloy under alkaline conditions, lower dissolution was observed. Still, the improvement was not striking and can be rather explained by the lowered concentration of elements in the multinary alloys instead of the synergistic effects of thermodynamics.
